correctness.rationale: Defant's Schemmel formula gives L₂(1)=1, L₂(n)=0 for even n and L₂(n)=∏p^(a−1)(p−2) for odd n. An even n>1 stops at zero and cannot be fixed; an odd n>1 maps to an odd strictly smaller integer, so with D₂(1)=0 the sum of iterates really is L₂(n)+D₂(L₂(n)). The frozen linear sieve assigns least primes by their unique generating pair (n/p,p), and the two odd recurrence branches correctly account for whether p already divides n/p. The intermediate products and accumulated sums fit the stated integer types (even the bound N(N−1)/2 fits int64). Independently implemented segmented odd factor stripping with trial primes up to √N: for each odd input k the array starts at k, applies the exact integer operation /p·(p−2) once per distinct processed prime, and uses the stripped residual (1 or one prime) for the last factor. In increasing order an independent array then accumulates D₂. The replay visited all 49,999,999 odd inputs 3≤k≤10⁸; the even inputs are excluded by the formula. It gave [37147, 53290831], π=5761455 and diagnostic maximum 284911615 at 97556803. Replay: python3 -B /workspace/audit-evidence/1_segmented_odd_sieve.py 100000000 (NumPy integer vectors); prefix and terminal outputs in /workspace/audit-evidence/1_replay.txt. This is finite, not a global uniqueness assertion.

value.rationale: Defant explicitly asks about additional fixed points and comments on their scant data. The decimal cutoff 10⁸ is the first power of ten beyond the previously recorded second example, three decimal orders beyond the primary paper's 10⁵-scale search. An exact interval containing both and excluding any others is a useful reproducible baseline for further distribution or search work, not discovery of the two examples or evidence of global uniqueness.
